nodes.title: TAXONOMY
nodes.body:
Common Name: Gulf Killifish
Scientific Name: Fundulus grandis

nodes.title: Classification
nodes.body:
Phylum:  Chordata
	Class:  Osteichthyes
	Order:  Atheriniformes
	Family:  Cyprinodontidae

Other Common Names:  mummichog, mud minnow, chub, saltwater minnow, bull minnow

Other:	Reference for Scientific Name (Baird and Girard 1853).
	Reference for Classification (1914)

nodes.title: VALUE & STATUS
nodes.body:
Commercial:  Sold as bait for flounder, red drum, sand trout and spotted seatrout (Hoese and Moore 1977; 2503; 2502).

Recreational:  Caught for bait by recreational fisherman (2503).

Ecological Role:  This is an abundant euryhaline marsh resident of the Gulf of Mexico and east coast of Florida, which feeds on a variety of marsh invertebrates and is a rapacious consumer of mosquito larvae as natural food source (664; 2426, 1982; 1862; 2430; 2422) and is subsequently consumed by piscivorous fishes and birds (2430; 2503).  In the marginal wetlands of the Indian River Lagoon and south Florida it is considered a keystone species along with the marsh killifish, sheepshead minnow, eastern mosquitofish and sailfin molly.

Indicator:  This species depends on fresh or salt water marsh habitat (664).  Its eggs withstand seasonal exposure before marsh flooding (2425; 2503).  Apparently there is dependency on tidal and natural seasonal water fluctuations as marsh impoundment eradicates this species (2367; 2363).  Therefore, the absence of this species from previously inhabited salt marshes is a good indicator of changes in natural flooding patterns, particularly when associated with marsh impoundment.  Fundulus grandis has been used commonly for ichthyonoxicity and ichthyotoxicity evaluations through bioassays (2472; 2488; 2485; 2487).

nodes.title: GEOGRAPHIC RANGE
nodes.body:
Overall: Occurs in northeastern Florida from the Matanzas River south around peninsula Florida, the eastern, northern and western Gulf of Mexico south to Laguna de Tamiahua, south of Tampico, Veracruz, Mexico (2490; 2421; 2365; 2493).

Within Study Area: Along vegetated and sandy beaches, marginal wetlands and low marsh tidal creek habitats throughout the Indian River Lagoon (2426; 848).  The Gulf killifish is most abundant in salt marshes of the northern half of the Indian River Lagoon north of 28 00'N. (2386; 2320; 2362).

nodes.title: Life Mode
nodes.body:
Egg: eggs are benthic and epiphytic and deposited on a semilunar cycle throughout a prolonged spawning period from late winter to late fall.
Larvae: larvae are epibenthic, spending early development in shallow marginal wetlands (2426; 2478; 2503; 2479; 2480; 2482, 2483).
Juvenile: juveniles are usually diurnally active in schools feeding over sand or mud bottoms in shallow marsh habitats and have been observed to congregate after dark in large numbers in shallows next to litter blown against mangrove pneumatophores at water's edge (2426).
Adult: adults same as Juveniles. Spawning is nocturnal amongst emergent vegetation (2474).

Mobility and Migration:
Adults and juveniles make local migrations onto high marsh surface (intertidal) associated with water level changes then retreat to deeper subtidal creeks and vegetated marginal areas of salt marsh (2426; 2478; 2503; 2494).

nodes.title: Habitat Type
nodes.body:
Egg: eggs are benthic or epiphytic, laid on blades of cordgrass, Spartina alterniflora, blackrush, Juncus romoerianus, sea-ox-eye, Borrichia frutescens or on oyster shells and other benthic objects (2493).  Eggs withstand exposure two weeks between spring tides or rainwater flooding of the wetland vegetation (2425; 2478; 2503; 2479; 2482, 1989).
Juvenile: juveniles forage diurnally over open bottoms, high marsh flats and along marginal salt and brackish marsh vegetation along tidal creeks.  Foraging efficiency is high with greatest volume of food consumed when on intertidal marsh flats rather than within subtidal creeks (2494).
Adult: Same as juveniles.

Substrate:  Juveniles and adults occur over sand, mud, detrital and algal bottoms near emergent wetland vegetation (2494).

nodes.title: Physical/Chemical
nodes.body:
Temperature: temperatures of 10.4-33.0 C (664; 2426; 2503).  Constant high temperatures over 26 C. inhibit gonadal maturation (2475) while constant temperatures of 30 C cause male gonadal regression (Greeley and MacGregor 1978).

Salinity: This is a euryhaline species occurring in abundance in highly saline barrier island salt marshes to coastal tidal freshwater river and creek systems (2372; 2493).  Recorded from salinities of 0.00-76.1 ppt (2497); preferred salinities of 10-20 ppt (664). Preferred salinities of 5-40 ppt were indicated in hatching viability studies of Waas (1982) and (2492).

nodes.title: REPRODUCTION
nodes.body:
Reproductive Mode: gonochoristic, polygamous, oviparous, and iteroparous; eggs are fertilized externally (2478; 2503).

Mating/Spawning:  Spawning occurs in emergent shoreline vegetation (ex. Spartina spp.) from late winter to late fall and is dependent on water temperature (255; 2497; 664; Greeley and MacGregor 1978, 2478; 2503; 2479; 2482, 1989).  Commencement of spawning is controlled by photoperiod (gen. 11-12 hrs of daylight) rather than temperature (2489; 2503).  Semilunar and diel spawning activity is controlled by a combination of endogenous and environmental stimuli (2479; 2482, 2483).  Mating occurs on highest spring tide with egg deposition on vegetation or other protected substrates as the male clasps and presses the female against the substrate during the deposition of 10 - 20 eggs (2421 & b; 2493; 2503).

Fecundity: Wild Gulf killifish fecundities vary from 121 to 758 eggs when ripe (2503).

nodes.title: Length Range
nodes.body:
Egg:  Eggs are demersal, spherical, with chorionic bristles and filaments and 2.02-2.09 mm in diameter after fertilization (2421; 2503).  Yolk with 10-15 oil globules in mature egg.  Ovarian/ovulated eggs average diameter of 2.09 mm at maturation (2503).  Eggs hatch between 16.3 and 22.3 d at 0 to 80 ppt salinities and temperature of 19 C. (2492), 9-14 d at 26-31 C/30 ppt, 14-28 d at 12.5 -33 C/5-10 ppt, 21 d at 20 C (2484; 2499, 2500; 2501; 2472).  Eggs withstand exposure on blades of emergent vegetation for up to two weeks, between spring tides (2478; 2503).  The eggs hatch after 16-22 days of constant submergence or within minutes if reimmersion (2424) and larvae are epibenthic in the same habitat as eggs (2478).

Larvae:  Larvae are 7.0 mm TL at hatching (2492).  There is no information on larval-juvenile transition size in F. grandis, however, it may be assumed to be very similar to F. heteroclitus which is 25 mm SL (2486).  Duration of larval stage unknown, but may be assumed to be less than two weeks based on captive and wild growth rate data for F. grandis (664; 2499).

Juvenile:  There is no information for F. grandis, however using F. heteroclitus as a model juveniles may range from 25 to 28 mm SL in females, to 32 mm SL in males, with maturation possibly occurring during the same year of spawning (2473; 312; 2496).

Adults:  Pond raised Gulf killifish may reach a mean SL of 56 mm within 52 d at temperatures of 22-35.5C, salinities of 11-16 ppt (2499).  Wild fish in class II average 68 mm SL in Tampa Bay attaining reproductive maturity during this period at 40 to 50 mm TL (664).  Adults may survive into class III and IV, possibly yr 2 and reach 141 mm TL (664).

nodes.title: FOOD HABITS
nodes.body:
Larvae: larvae feed predominately on microcrustaceans (calanoid and harpacticoid copepods) and mosquito larvae (Aedes spp; 2426; 1862).
Juvenile: juveniles (25-40 mm SL) are omnivores with a strong bias toward carnivory with insects, mostly larval mosquitos making up the majority of the diet (2426).
Adult: diet of adults is diverse, consisting primarily of crustaceans (ex. hermit crabs, palaemonid shrimp, Tanaids and amphipods), molluscs (ex. gastropods and pelecypods), polychaetes and various fishes (ex. Poecilia latipinna, Brevoortia patronus, Fundulus grandis, F. majalis, Cyprinodon variegatus, Gambusia affinis {= holbrooki} and Gobiosoma sp.)(664; 2426; 2476; 1862; 2495; 2498; 2493; 2494).  Foraging occurs primarily on flood tidal inundations of the intertidal marsh plane rather than in subtidal creeks (2494).

nodes.title: ECOLOGICAL INTERACTIONS
nodes.body:
Predation:  Due to its abundance in estuaries and marginal wetlands in south Florida  it is highly likely that the Gulf killifish plays an important role as prey for wetland predators, wading birds, cormorants, semi-aquatic reptiles, spotted seatrout, sand seatrout, red drum, flounder,  snook, tarpon and ladyfish (2430; 2503; 2422).  In addition, it is a principal predator of salt marsh fish and invertebrate faunas of the intertidal zone (2494).

Factors Influencing Populations:  Gulf killifish populations depend on marginal wetland vegetation and structures for egg deposition (2421; 2493).  Therefore, removal of marginal vegetation will impact the reproductive capacity of this species.  The Gulf killifish also requires water level fluctuations for optimum reproduction and foraging in intertidal zones of marginal wetlands.  If periodically flooded intertidal wetlands are reduced due to upland development, sea level rise, etc. habitat and resources for this species will also be reduced. Under natural conditions predation probably plays the most significant role in influencing population abundance.

sections.heading: HEADER
sections.content:
Title: Gulf Killifish (Fundulus grandis)

FLELMR Code:  1406

sections.heading: Revisions
sections.content: 1994. R. Grant Gilmore, Harbor Branch Oceanographic Institution, Florida.

sections.heading: TAXONOMY
sections.content:
Common Name: Gulf Killifish
Scientific Name: Fundulus grandis

sections.heading: Classification
sections.content:
Phylum:  Chordata
	Class:  Osteichthyes
	Order:  Atheriniformes
	Family:  Cyprinodontidae

Other Common Names:  mummichog, mud minnow, chub, saltwater minnow, bull minnow

Other:	Reference for Scientific Name (Baird and Girard 1853).
	Reference for Classification (1914)

sections.heading: VALUE & STATUS
sections.content:
Commercial:  Sold as bait for flounder, red drum, sand trout and spotted seatrout (Hoese and Moore 1977; 2503; 2502).

Recreational:  Caught for bait by recreational fisherman (2503).

Ecological Role:  This is an abundant euryhaline marsh resident of the Gulf of Mexico and east coast of Florida, which feeds on a variety of marsh invertebrates and is a rapacious consumer of mosquito larvae as natural food source (664; 2426, 1982; 1862; 2430; 2422) and is subsequently consumed by piscivorous fishes and birds (2430; 2503).  In the marginal wetlands of the Indian River Lagoon and south Florida it is considered a keystone species along with the marsh killifish, sheepshead minnow, eastern mosquitofish and sailfin molly.

Indicator:  This species depends on fresh or salt water marsh habitat (664).  Its eggs withstand seasonal exposure before marsh flooding (2425; 2503).  Apparently there is dependency on tidal and natural seasonal water fluctuations as marsh impoundment eradicates this species (2367; 2363).  Therefore, the absence of this species from previously inhabited salt marshes is a good indicator of changes in natural flooding patterns, particularly when associated with marsh impoundment.  Fundulus grandis has been used commonly for ichthyonoxicity and ichthyotoxicity evaluations through bioassays (2472; 2488; 2485; 2487).

sections.heading: GEOGRAPHIC RANGE
sections.content:
Overall: Occurs in northeastern Florida from the Matanzas River south around peninsula Florida, the eastern, northern and western Gulf of Mexico south to Laguna de Tamiahua, south of Tampico, Veracruz, Mexico (2490; 2421; 2365; 2493).

Within Study Area: Along vegetated and sandy beaches, marginal wetlands and low marsh tidal creek habitats throughout the Indian River Lagoon (2426; 848).  The Gulf killifish is most abundant in salt marshes of the northern half of the Indian River Lagoon north of 28 00'N. (2386; 2320; 2362).

sections.heading: Life Mode
sections.content:
Egg: eggs are benthic and epiphytic and deposited on a semilunar cycle throughout a prolonged spawning period from late winter to late fall.
Larvae: larvae are epibenthic, spending early development in shallow marginal wetlands (2426; 2478; 2503; 2479; 2480; 2482, 2483).
Juvenile: juveniles are usually diurnally active in schools feeding over sand or mud bottoms in shallow marsh habitats and have been observed to congregate after dark in large numbers in shallows next to litter blown against mangrove pneumatophores at water's edge (2426).
Adult: adults same as Juveniles. Spawning is nocturnal amongst emergent vegetation (2474).

Mobility and Migration:
Adults and juveniles make local migrations onto high marsh surface (intertidal) associated with water level changes then retreat to deeper subtidal creeks and vegetated marginal areas of salt marsh (2426; 2478; 2503; 2494).

sections.heading: Habitat Type
sections.content:
Egg: eggs are benthic or epiphytic, laid on blades of cordgrass, Spartina alterniflora, blackrush, Juncus romoerianus, sea-ox-eye, Borrichia frutescens or on oyster shells and other benthic objects (2493).  Eggs withstand exposure two weeks between spring tides or rainwater flooding of the wetland vegetation (2425; 2478; 2503; 2479; 2482, 1989).
Juvenile: juveniles forage diurnally over open bottoms, high marsh flats and along marginal salt and brackish marsh vegetation along tidal creeks.  Foraging efficiency is high with greatest volume of food consumed when on intertidal marsh flats rather than within subtidal creeks (2494).
Adult: Same as juveniles.

Substrate:  Juveniles and adults occur over sand, mud, detrital and algal bottoms near emergent wetland vegetation (2494).

sections.heading: Physical/Chemical
sections.content:
Temperature: temperatures of 10.4-33.0 C (664; 2426; 2503).  Constant high temperatures over 26 C. inhibit gonadal maturation (2475) while constant temperatures of 30 C cause male gonadal regression (Greeley and MacGregor 1978).

Salinity: This is a euryhaline species occurring in abundance in highly saline barrier island salt marshes to coastal tidal freshwater river and creek systems (2372; 2493).  Recorded from salinities of 0.00-76.1 ppt (2497); preferred salinities of 10-20 ppt (664). Preferred salinities of 5-40 ppt were indicated in hatching viability studies of Waas (1982) and (2492).

sections.heading: REPRODUCTION
sections.content:
Reproductive Mode: gonochoristic, polygamous, oviparous, and iteroparous; eggs are fertilized externally (2478; 2503).

Mating/Spawning:  Spawning occurs in emergent shoreline vegetation (ex. Spartina spp.) from late winter to late fall and is dependent on water temperature (255; 2497; 664; Greeley and MacGregor 1978, 2478; 2503; 2479; 2482, 1989).  Commencement of spawning is controlled by photoperiod (gen. 11-12 hrs of daylight) rather than temperature (2489; 2503).  Semilunar and diel spawning activity is controlled by a combination of endogenous and environmental stimuli (2479; 2482, 2483).  Mating occurs on highest spring tide with egg deposition on vegetation or other protected substrates as the male clasps and presses the female against the substrate during the deposition of 10 - 20 eggs (2421 & b; 2493; 2503).

Fecundity: Wild Gulf killifish fecundities vary from 121 to 758 eggs when ripe (2503).

sections.heading: Length Range
sections.content:
Egg:  Eggs are demersal, spherical, with chorionic bristles and filaments and 2.02-2.09 mm in diameter after fertilization (2421; 2503).  Yolk with 10-15 oil globules in mature egg.  Ovarian/ovulated eggs average diameter of 2.09 mm at maturation (2503).  Eggs hatch between 16.3 and 22.3 d at 0 to 80 ppt salinities and temperature of 19 C. (2492), 9-14 d at 26-31 C/30 ppt, 14-28 d at 12.5 -33 C/5-10 ppt, 21 d at 20 C (2484; 2499, 2500; 2501; 2472).  Eggs withstand exposure on blades of emergent vegetation for up to two weeks, between spring tides (2478; 2503).  The eggs hatch after 16-22 days of constant submergence or within minutes if reimmersion (2424) and larvae are epibenthic in the same habitat as eggs (2478).

Larvae:  Larvae are 7.0 mm TL at hatching (2492).  There is no information on larval-juvenile transition size in F. grandis, however, it may be assumed to be very similar to F. heteroclitus which is 25 mm SL (2486).  Duration of larval stage unknown, but may be assumed to be less than two weeks based on captive and wild growth rate data for F. grandis (664; 2499).

Juvenile:  There is no information for F. grandis, however using F. heteroclitus as a model juveniles may range from 25 to 28 mm SL in females, to 32 mm SL in males, with maturation possibly occurring during the same year of spawning (2473; 312; 2496).

Adults:  Pond raised Gulf killifish may reach a mean SL of 56 mm within 52 d at temperatures of 22-35.5C, salinities of 11-16 ppt (2499).  Wild fish in class II average 68 mm SL in Tampa Bay attaining reproductive maturity during this period at 40 to 50 mm TL (664).  Adults may survive into class III and IV, possibly yr 2 and reach 141 mm TL (664).

sections.heading: FOOD HABITS
sections.content:
Larvae: larvae feed predominately on microcrustaceans (calanoid and harpacticoid copepods) and mosquito larvae (Aedes spp; 2426; 1862).
Juvenile: juveniles (25-40 mm SL) are omnivores with a strong bias toward carnivory with insects, mostly larval mosquitos making up the majority of the diet (2426).
Adult: diet of adults is diverse, consisting primarily of crustaceans (ex. hermit crabs, palaemonid shrimp, Tanaids and amphipods), molluscs (ex. gastropods and pelecypods), polychaetes and various fishes (ex. Poecilia latipinna, Brevoortia patronus, Fundulus grandis, F. majalis, Cyprinodon variegatus, Gambusia affinis {= holbrooki} and Gobiosoma sp.)(664; 2426; 2476; 1862; 2495; 2498; 2493; 2494).  Foraging occurs primarily on flood tidal inundations of the intertidal marsh plane rather than in subtidal creeks (2494).

sections.heading: ECOLOGICAL INTERACTIONS
sections.content:
Predation:  Due to its abundance in estuaries and marginal wetlands in south Florida  it is highly likely that the Gulf killifish plays an important role as prey for wetland predators, wading birds, cormorants, semi-aquatic reptiles, spotted seatrout, sand seatrout, red drum, flounder,  snook, tarpon and ladyfish (2430; 2503; 2422).  In addition, it is a principal predator of salt marsh fish and invertebrate faunas of the intertidal zone (2494).

Factors Influencing Populations:  Gulf killifish populations depend on marginal wetland vegetation and structures for egg deposition (2421; 2493).  Therefore, removal of marginal vegetation will impact the reproductive capacity of this species.  The Gulf killifish also requires water level fluctuations for optimum reproduction and foraging in intertidal zones of marginal wetlands.  If periodically flooded intertidal wetlands are reduced due to upland development, sea level rise, etc. habitat and resources for this species will also be reduced. Under natural conditions predation probably plays the most significant role in influencing population abundance.
